name: Te Wāhipounamu
blurb: Beech rainforest, takahe and kiwi, and the introduced stoats that hunt them.

tip.title: Trigger a beech seed year
tip.text: Silver beech seed feeds mice, and mice feed stoats. Raise Silver beech and watch mice and stoats climb, then takahe and kiwi come under pressure.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Westerly rain
nodes.desc: Moist westerly winds off the Tasman Sea drop more than seven metres of rain a year on much of the park, feeding the temperate rainforest.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest canopy and the sunlit surface of the fiords powers the plants and algae at the base of the web.

nodes.name: Fiord seawater
nodes.desc: Glaciers carved deep fiords along the coast, and their cool, steep-sided waters feed the marine plankton.

nodes.name: Forest soil and litter
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and soil hold the nutrients that the rainforest trees draw back up.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and dead animals, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Silver beech
nodes.desc: A dominant tree of Fiordland forests. Its heavy seed years feed rodent booms that in turn feed stoats.

nodes.name: Broadleaf
nodes.desc: A common native forest tree whose leaves and fruit are eaten by browsing mammals and forest birds.

nodes.name: Southern rata
nodes.desc: A flowering tree of the southern forests. Possums are recorded eating its foliage.

nodes.name: Snow tussock
nodes.desc: Tall alpine tussock grasses. Their leaves are the main food of takahe and are also grazed by red deer.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae in the sunlit surface water of the fiords and the sea beyond.

nodes.name: Red deer
nodes.desc: Introduced browser that damages forest and alpine vegetation and competes with takahe for food.

nodes.name: Common brushtail possum
nodes.desc: Introduced from Australia. It eats the leaves of native trees and continues to damage the forest.

nodes.name: Takahe
nodes.desc: Large flightless rail rediscovered in the Murchison Mountains in 1948. It eats mainly the leaves of snow tussock.

nodes.name: New Zealand bellbird
nodes.desc: A common forest bird that feeds on nectar, fruit and insects.

nodes.name: Kea
nodes.desc: Alpine parrot that eats roots, leaves, berries and insects, and also scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: House mouse
nodes.desc: Introduced rodent whose numbers jump after heavy beech seed years, which then draws in stoats.

nodes.name: Leaf-eating insects
nodes.desc: Beetles, caterpillars and other insects feeding on forest foliage; food for birds.

nodes.name: Krill
nodes.desc: Small shrimp-like crustaceans that graze plankton and feed fish, seabirds and whales.

nodes.name: Southern brown kiwi
nodes.desc: Flightless forest bird found almost entirely in Fiordland and nearby areas; it probes soil for invertebrates.

nodes.name: Fiordland crested penguin
nodes.desc: Nests in coastal rainforest and feeds at sea, mostly on squid, krill and some fish.

nodes.name: Swamp harrier
nodes.desc: Bird of prey recorded eating possums and rabbits; it hunts and scavenges across open ground.

nodes.name: Stoat
nodes.desc: Introduced predator of forest birds including kiwi and takahe. Numbers surge after beech seed years.
